extracted.intended_audience: students, historians of mathematics, and mathematically literate general readers interested in the history and foundations of calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Cauchy's foundational definitions and approach to making calculus rigorous (limits, infinitesimals, continuity, convergence, derivative, mean value theorem) as presented in his Cours d'Analyse (1821).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to rigor / avoidance of algebraic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: As for my methods, I have sought to give them all the rigour which is demanded in geometry, in such a way as never to fall back on reasons drawn from what is usually described in algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy argues algebraic manipulations are inductive and can suggest formulas have unlimited generality when they are valid only under certain conditions; one should determine those conditions and fix precisely the sense of all notations to remove uncertainty. This is presented as a methodological criterion for rigorous calculus: prefer geometric-style rigour and precise hypotheses over informal algebraic inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a limit
rubrics_metrics.description: When the values successively attributed to the same variable approach indefinitely a fixed value, eventually differing from it by as little as one could wish, that fixed value is called the limit of all the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Cauchy's working definition of limit: a variable's successive values approaching a fixed value arbitrarily closely. It underpins his treatment of continuity, derivatives, and series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an infinitesimal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the successive absolute values of a variable decrease indefinitely in such a way as to become less than any given quantity, that variable becomes what is called an infinitesimal. Such a variable has zero for its limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinitesimals are variables whose absolute values become arbitrarily small; Cauchy treats them as having limit zero and uses them in defining continuity and derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of continuity (infinitesimal formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function f(x) will be a continuous function of this variable within the two limits assigned to the variable x if, for every value of x between these limits, the absolute value of the difference f(x+a) - f(x) decreases indefinitely with that of a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: between the given limits, an infinitely small increment of the variable always produces an infinitely small increment of the function itself. Cauchy uses this infinitesimal-dependent formulation to prove examples such as sin x being continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of convergence and sum of a series (Cauchy criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S_n = u_0 + u_1 + ... + u_{n-1} be the sum of the first n terms. If, for increasing values of n, the sum S_n approaches a certain limit S, the series will be called convergent and the limit in question will be called the sum of the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy notes S_{n+1}-S_n = u_n, S_{n+2}-S_n = u_n+u_{n+1}, etc. He states it is necessary (but not sufficient) that u_n has limit zero, and additionally necessary that tails (sums of u_n, u_{n+1}, ...) have absolute values arbitrarily small; conversely, when these conditions are satisfied convergence is assured. This is the Cauchy-style criterion about control of tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the derivative (derived function as limit of difference quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one puts Dx = i, the two terms of the ratio of differences Dy/Dx = (f(x+i) - f(x))/i will be infinitely small quantities. ... the ratio itself can converge towards another limit ... this limit, when it exists, has a definite value for each particular value of x; ... one gives the new function the name derived function, and designates it ... by f'(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy defines the derivative as the limit (when it exists) of the difference quotient formed with an infinitesimal increment i. The derivative is treated as a new function depending on x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's version of the mean value theorem (inequality form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) is continuous between the limits x = a and x = b, we designate by A the smallest and by B the largest value that the derived function f'(x) attains in the interval, the ratio of the finite differences (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a) will necessarily be included between A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a bound on the average rate of change by the extreme values of the derivative on the interval; it's a formulation of the mean value principle in inequality form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations / counterexamples to Cauchy's claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy 'proved' incorrectly that the limit of a convergent series of continuous functions is continuous. Abel produced a counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a cautionary note: Cauchy's definitions and methods, while aiming at rigour, were not fully sufficient to prevent incorrect theorems in some contexts (here, interchange of limit and continuity). It highlights the need for stronger hypotheses (uniform convergence, etc.) not present in Cauchy's formulation.
